newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Fantozzi sees broad EMU if French left wins.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fantozzi sees broad EMU if French left wins.

text.p: Italy's foreign trade minister, in the first Italian government reaction to the left's breakthrough in the first round of French elections, said on Monday the result could open the way to fresh discussions and flexible interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for a single currency.
Augusto Fantozzi, visiting France for talks at the OECD, said the left's gains also pointed to a large number of countries signing up to monetary union in the first wave.

"The French elections show that you have to be careful on the way to Europe," Fantozzi told a news conference. "It shows that additional discussions will be required between France and ... other countries about the Maastricht criteria."
The French left's lead "probably will make evaluation of the (Maastricht) criteria more flexible," he said, adding that the final result of the snap parliamentary election was unknown.
"It shows that we have to be in a large number of countries joining EMU at the very beginning," he said, adding "Italy will be with the first, I can't say when".
He gave no indication whether he was talking of a possible delay in the 1999 launch date for European monetary union.

Fantozzi's remarks in English to reporters at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development were the first public reaction by an Italian government minister to the left's upset first-round victory in France on Sunday.
The result had earlier been warmly welcomed by the Democratic Party of the Left, the dominant force of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's ruling coalition.
Official results showed the combined left polled 40.22 percent of the vote in Sunday's first round of voting for France's the National Assembly, or lower house of parliament.
The centre-right RPR-UDF coalition and other moderate rightists scored 36.50 percent and the extreme-right National Front 14.94 percent. Ecologists scored 6.81 percent.
Most seats will go to a second decisive ballot on June 1.
Fantozzi declined to comment on conditions for EMU laid down by opposition Socialists during the French election campaign.
The conditions include early entry for Italy and Spain to the single currency and an "economic government" as a counterweight to the European central bank.

But he said his sense of the results so far was that "it puts attention on the internal opinion of the French (electorate) being sceptical on EMU, and this will draw attention to the national opinions of all countries involved".
"EMU is essential and Italy will be among the first (to join)," he said.

Prodi has said he is determined to take Italy into the euro at the start. His government is battling to slash its budget deficit by the end of the year to join the first wave of nations in the single currency at the start of 1999.
